title: The Dragon and the Demigod
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
Maui had a plan involving a wall of fire.

I knew because he spread his arms across the Jasmine Dragon's counter and described it in tremendous detail while Iroh continued pouring tea with the expression of someone who had already heard three worse plans before breakfast.

"Imagine the lanterns," Maui said. "All lighting at once. A giant flame across the terraces, then the whole sky—"

"No," I said.

"I haven't finished."

"That's why I'm saying it now."

Iroh set down the kettle.

"Perhaps we should begin with what the festival requires."

"Joy," Maui declared.

"Yes."

"Wonder."

"Certainly."

"A little fire."

"Some," Iroh said, "would be permissible in a properly contained lamp."

Maui looked betrayed.

We were preparing the closing evening of the Longlight season, when residents hung the last of the wind-marker kites and lit low-smoke lanterns along the safe route. The storm had damaged several garden steps, and Tamsin had posted a clear fire and load plan. Open flame was permitted only inside protected lantern housings away from dry cloth and the old timber supports.

Maui had apparently seen the word permitted and taken it as an artistic challenge.

"People like spectacle," he said.

"People also like having roofs," I answered.

Iroh smiled.

"Both are worth considering."

We took the plan to Tamsin, who was checking a repaired gutter outside the teahouse. She listened for exactly forty seconds before taking the paper and circling three places where flame would be too close to cloth, one where the walkway was too narrow, and another where heat could damage a wooden railing.

"That," she said, handing it back, "is a list of things not to do."

Maui frowned.

"You're all very difficult."

"We are trying to remain alive," I said.

Iroh looked at the drawings.

"What is it you want people to feel when the lanterns are lit?" he asked.

Maui hesitated. Then he spread his arms as though he could fit the entire village between them.

"I want them to look up! I want them to say, 'Whoa, did the great Maui do that?'" He caught Iroh's expression. "Fine, yes, and I want the kids who hauled those boards to see this place can still be spectacular. Is it a crime to want both?"

Iroh's expression softened.

"Then let us make something memorable that doesn't ask anyone to stand beneath falling fire."

We moved the planning meeting to the garden.

Iroh brought a box of shallow metal trays, polished on the inside. He set one beside a lantern and angled it toward the wall. The small flame reflected across the curved surface, making a broad patch of warm light.

Maui leaned closer.

"That's clever."

"It is a simple trick of light," Iroh said.

"Still clever."

I took another tray and tried the angle. My first attempt sent the reflection directly into Iroh's eyes.

He blinked.

"Perhaps a little lower."

"Sorry."

Maui laughed.

We spent the afternoon testing the arrangement. With six lanterns and six reflectors, we could illuminate the old stone wall without adding more heat than the fire plan allowed. The metal would cool before being packed away. The accessible route remained clear.

Pip suggested small carved shapes in front of the reflectors, so the light made moving shadows on the wall when the breeze reached the lantern housings.

Maui drew a fish.

I drew a star.

Iroh drew a very round teapot.

"That is a dangerous creature," Maui said solemnly.

"It has defeated many impatient men," Iroh replied.

I laughed.

At dusk, the volunteers tested the display. The light spread across the stone in overlapping gold shapes. A fish swam slowly through the shadow of a star. The teapot appeared to steam, though the effect was only light moving through a little paper cutout.

Children gathered beneath the shelter and pointed.

Maui watched their faces.

He looked almost as pleased as he would have if the sky had caught fire.

"Better than the giant flame?" I whispered.

He considered.

"Different."

"Safer."

"Very different."

Iroh stepped beside him.

"One does not have to become smaller to give someone else room to see."

Maui looked at him.

"Was that wisdom?"

"Only an observation."

"You're suspiciously good at those."

Iroh smiled.

The argument moved outside while Pip checked the screens. Maui leaned against the courtyard wall and looked at Iroh as though the older man had committed a personal insult.

"You're really going to light the whole thing with ordinary lamps?"

"They are lamps with an excellent history of lighting things," Iroh replied.

"Where's the spectacle?"

"In the shadow someone wishes to show."

Maui made a dissatisfied noise. I was about to intervene when Iroh held up a hand—not to silence either of us, but to ask for a moment.

"Tell me something, Maui. When you learned to pull an island from the sea, did you know who would live there?"

Maui stared at him. His tattoos shifted over his arm. "Not everyone."

"Then perhaps a lantern belongs to whoever uses its light, not to whoever can make the brightest flame."

I winced. It was sharper than Iroh usually sounded. Maui heard it too.

"That's a pretty way to tell me to shut up."

Iroh closed his eyes for a moment. "It was a pretty way to avoid apologizing for having been rude."

I looked between them. That admission mattered more than the proverb.

Maui rubbed the back of his neck. "I wasn't listening to Pip. I heard a festival and imagined a crowd chanting my name."

"An understandable temptation," Iroh said.

"Oh, you want applause too?"

"Certainly. When the jasmine cakes rise properly, I am insufferable."

Maui laughed so loudly that someone inside asked whether the screen frame had fallen.

I took a step toward him, then stopped. I loved both men. I'd told each of them plainly that I was ethically non-monogamous and preferred polyamory; I didn't want that to make me an interpreter for every conflict they chose to have.

"Work it out between you," I said. "Pip still needs the lamps."

Maui held out his hand to Iroh. "I'll carry them."

Iroh took it. "I'll ask where they should go."

They went inside without asking me to decide who had been wiser. I stood in the courtyard for another breath, smelling hot paper and tea, and felt the strange relief of not being responsible for making two people I loved agree.

Before the public was invited inside, Pip asked us to test the screens once more. A paper edge had curled near a candle. Nobody had been hurt, but the demonstration wasn't going to open while somebody could brush a hand against hot paper.

Maui opened his mouth. I could almost see his argument assembling itself: he could move fire safely, he had faced the sea, he had personally solved problems much larger than this.

Iroh put a hand on his arm. "Let them finish."

Maui looked betrayed. Then he glanced at the child standing beside the frame, clutching a paper boat they'd made.

"Will it be all right?" the child asked.

"After we move the lamp," Pip answered. "If you'd like, you can help choose where your boat's shadow goes."

"Only for one song."

"Then only for one song."

We adjusted the frame and waited for it to cool. Maui held the little boat as carefully as if it were made of glass. He asked the child whether the shadow looked right. The child shook their head, so he moved it to the left.

"Better?"

"Perfect."

I laughed at the pride on his face. Iroh leaned close enough to speak quietly.

"You chose well when you told him the sky did not need catching fire," he said.

"I chose self-preservation. We'd still be arguing about insurance."

He chuckled.

A vendor came to ask whether we wanted more lantern oil. Pip checked the inventory before agreeing to buy enough for the scheduled display. Nobody was being asked to donate supplies they hadn't promised. The little festival felt less magical for all its lists and receipts, but it was also less likely to leave someone cleaning up alone at midnight.

Iroh touched my hand. "Will you stay beside me for the opening?"

"Yes. Afterward I'm helping Maui and the children put away the reflectors."

"I know."

"You don't mind?"

"I may wish I had more time. That is different from claiming yours."

I smiled at him. We'd spoken openly about my being ethically non-monogamous and preferring polyamory. Our relationships were chosen, not ranked, and neither man had to pretend to feel nothing about sharing time.

"Then I'll find you when the last lantern goes out," I said.

"With tea?"

"With tea."

He glanced at my mouth, then asked if he might kiss me before the crowd arrived. I stepped closer. His kiss was slow and warm, with the faint taste of jasmine that always seemed to linger on his lips.

When we parted, Maui was balancing the child's boat on one finger.

"Don't," I called.

"I wasn't!"

The obvious lie made us all laugh, including the child. The little boat survived the evening, and so did the paper screens.

At rehearsal, Maui lifted a polished reflector so high that its beam flashed straight into a child's eyes.

“Put it down,” Iroh said.

His voice was quiet and absolute. Maui obeyed before remembering he had not agreed to take orders.

“Hey! I know how to hold a piece of metal.”

“And the child knows how it feels to be dazzled by it,” Iroh replied.

Tamsin turned the reflector toward the ground while Pip checked on the child. I watched Iroh realize how he had sounded. The Dragon of the West had arrived in the middle of a festival rehearsal, and not everybody was pleased to meet him.

“You don't command my hands,” Maui said.

“No,” Iroh answered. “The danger was real. The command was my mistake.”

Maui looked at the reflector and at Mini Maui, who had covered his tattooed face with both hands. “Okay. New plan. I carry it lower. The great Maui is capable of learning a thing or two.”

“Remarkable,” I murmured.

“I heard that!”

Iroh asked Tamsin to determine the safe angles rather than rearranging the display himself. Maui allowed a nine-year-old to choose the paper fish's position, although he announced the choice as though the child had just received an award.

The two men weren't interchangeable: Maui wanted the sky to notice; Iroh wanted to know who could get out if the lamps failed. Their better ideas came only after they let the people running the festival decide what was needed.


The display opened that evening. The first visitor asked how the shadows worked. Pip explained the reflectors. Another asked whether the light was magic. Iroh showed them the metal tray and let them examine it after it cooled.

Maui stayed at the side of the path, helping children place their own paper shapes at a safe distance from the lanterns.

No one needed to be dazzled into gratitude.

A child with a paper dragon approached while we were putting away the last screen. The painted wings had begun to curl from the damp, and the child was clutching it so hard the tail had crumpled.

“Is mine too small?” they asked Maui.

He looked from the dragon to the fish reflector he'd carried across the courtyard all afternoon. I knew that expression. He could make a dragon large enough to throw a shadow across the whole street, and some part of him wanted to do it immediately.

“Too small for what?” Iroh asked.

“To be seen.”

Iroh crouched to their level, careful not to put his own hand over the paper. “Where would you like its shadow to appear?”

The child pointed at the wall beside the bench. Maui examined the angle, then moved the reflector stand a little farther back. Pip came to check the clearance and asked them to use the cooler lantern rather than the candle closest to the paper.

I held the screen while the child unfolded the dragon's tail. When the lamp was lit, the shadow stretched across the plaster and looked almost enormous. The child squealed.

Maui drew himself up. “Well. A dragon of considerable distinction.”

“It looks like mine,” the child said.

“Of course it does,” Iroh answered.

Later, when the family collected the paper dragon, Maui tried to explain to me why the little shadow had been better than his first plan. His hands worked furiously in the air. He had no word for it that didn't sound like surrender.

“You can still make beautiful things,” I said. “You just don't need to make somebody else's dragon into your monument.”

He blinked. “I was going to say the fish looked better.”

“Then the fish looked better.”

Iroh's laugh reached us from the doorway. It was low and delighted, not the practiced voice of a man teaching a lesson. Maui spun toward him.

“You're on my side, General?”

“I am on the side of an excellent fish,” Iroh said, lifting a tray out of the path.

After the last lantern was extinguished, Iroh and I cleaned the trays. His sleeves were rolled to the elbow, and there was a little soot on his wrist.

"You're quiet," I said.

"I am enjoying the silence after so many questions."

"Did you mind working with Maui?"

"Not at all."

"Really?"

He laughed.

"He reminds me of people who once believed greatness required everyone to be looking at them."

I tilted my head.

"People you knew?"

"One or two."

"One of them you?"

His smile turned rueful.

"Possibly."

I dried the last tray.

"I love him," I said. "And I love you. I'm glad you can share a project without having to decide what that means for your relationship with each other."

Iroh took my hand.

"We are not required to be the same kind of companion to care for the same person."

The words warmed me more than the lanterns had.

He kissed my fingers, then waited while I moved closer.

"May I?" he asked.

"Please."

His kiss was gentle and a little amused, as though he'd found another secret worth keeping. The kitchen smelled of tea and soot, and the last lamp glowed beside the door.

The next morning, Maui delivered the reflectors back to storage with a handwritten note.

THANK YOU FOR LETTING THE FISH BE HEROIC.

Iroh pinned it above the worktable.

For weeks afterward, it made him smile.
